The open land is the heath, all heath. It runs on either side of the stream, and beyond it is the road. The road is bright and noisy, with cars and lights. The heath is dark and still, with heather and bracken and the scent of damp earth. I can see the road from my perch, and I hear the cars at night. They are not like the owls.

It is a field, dark with heather and dry grass. The road runs through it, with cars and lights. I do not like the lights. I hear the cars at night, and they scare the voles. The field is full of voles. I hunt them in the dark. I can hear them under the grass. I strike with my feet. I kill them with my beak. I eat them. The field is my hunting ground. I am the king of the field

The open land is the road. It runs through the wood, wide and dark, with cars that hiss and blink. They come at night, and the lights make the heath look like fire. I hear them from the oak, and I watch from the branches. The road is full of noise and danger. The heath is quiet, and the stream is cold. I prefer the heath.

The open land is the heath, all heath. It stretches beyond the stream and the lane, and beyond the farmland. It is dry and rough, with stones and brambles. The wind comes through it all the time, and the heath is full of voles. I hear them under the heath, scurrying in the dry grass. I can tell where they are by the sound. The open land is the heath. It is all heather and gorse, and the wind moves through it like a living thing. There are no trees, only the heath and the stream that runs by. In spring, the heather flowers and the ground is soft with moss. In winter, it is hard and bare, and the wind howls. I can hear the rabbits in the heath, and the voles in the stream. I fly low, over the heath, the stream, the lane. I follow the scent of voles, the rustle in the grass. I go where the light fades and the shadows grow. I do not go far. I know the wood well. I know where the voles are. I know where the mice are. I know where the beetles are. I know where the shrews are. I know where the worms are. I know where the crickets are.
From the hollow oak, up the trunk, into the branches. I keep the same route each night. I go over the heath, past the stream, and into the wood. I turn at the old ash and head back.

I fly to the edge of the wood, where the light fades and the shadows stretch. The mice come out then, and the voles. I glide low over the heath, the stream, the lane. I hear them in the grass, the roots, the undergrowth. I turn my head, my ears, and I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly over the heath, the stream, the lane. I follow the sounds. The mice in the grass, the voles in the field, the shrew in the hedgerow. I listen for the rustle, the squeak, the stir. I circle the oak, the ash, the birch. I hunt where the light fades, where the shadows grow. I find my prey in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
From the oak. I sit on the branch, then lift my head and wait for the light to go. Then I drop and fly. I fly straight, not much higher than the tree, and strike. I have a good view of the lane.

I fly out from the oak, circling the hollow, then out over the heath and the stream. I go low, skimming the heath and the stream, and look for the glint of a mouse or the movement of a shrew. I call as I go, "hoo-hoo-hooo," to let the others know where I am. I don't go far, not more than a mile, and I always come back to the oak. I hunt best in

I fly from the oak to the heath. The heath is full of voles, and the voles are full of mice. I follow the wind. If the wind carries the scent of mice, I fly low and hunt. If it carries the scent of a barn, I fly higher. I always fly east, where the light fades first. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
From the oak. I call from the oak, the heath is behind me, and the stream is ahead. I fly low, along the edge of the wood, and I turn up the stream. I call to the stream. The stream answers.

I fly to the edge of the wood, where the heath meets the lane. The light fades, and the voles come out. I glide low over the grass, listening for the rustle of a mouse under the leaves. Sometimes I circle the stream, where the water reflects the last of the daylight. I hunt by sound, not sight. The wind carries the scent of the earth, and I follow it. I am silent, and the voles do not hear me. Hoo

I fly straight up from the oak, then circle the wood, looking for the glint of a mouse or the rustle of a vole. I follow the light as it fades, and when it's gone, I go back to the oak. I don't hunt far. I hunt where I can see. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low, over the heath and the stream. I follow the light as it fades, the edges of the wood, the road where the voles come out. I listen for the rustle of leaves, the snap of a twig. I don't need to see much—my eyes are better in the dark. I go where the prey is, not where I want to be. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly from the oak to the wood edge, then out over the heath. I follow the light of the road, the flicker of the candles in the windows. I hunt voles and mice, and sometimes the scrawny ones that come up from the stream. I always return to the oak, where I can hear the wind and the owls. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
From the hollow oak, over the heath, past the stream, up the lane to the edge of the wood. I fly like a leaf.

I fly low, over the heath, the stream, the lane. I follow the light as it fades. I hunt voles, shrews, mice. I do not fly far, but I fly well. I call to my mate, and she calls back. I hear the rustle of leaves, the scuttle of a rodent. I strike. I eat. I return to the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

From the oak. I call up to the tree and fly out to the heath, the stream, the lane. I follow the sound of the vole. I do not know where I will land. I do not know where I will feed. I do not know where I will sleep. I just fly.
From the oak. I call first, then I fly. The heath, the lane, the stream bank. I go where the voles are. I can hear them under the leaves. I find them with my feet.
A long stretch of heath and then a stream. Beyond that, a road with lights and voices. I do not go there.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the heath, then the stream, then the lane, then the lights. I have not crossed the lane. The heath is dry and full of voles. The stream is cold and full of fish. The lane is quiet at night, but I hear the voices of the humans. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where it is safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of the wood is the heath. It is dry and windy, with no trees. The heath is where the rabbits are, and sometimes the foxes. I can hear them in the distance, but I do not go there. The heath is not safe. I stay in the wood, where it is quiet and dark. I do not know what lies beyond the heath, but I do not care. I have my owlet and my hollow. That is enough

The edge of my wood is the heath, all dry and heather and cold. Beyond that is the lane, where the lights blink and the cars go by. Then the road, and then the village with its windows and voices. I do not go beyond. The lane is too loud and the lights too bright. I stay in the wood, where the owls are and the voles are and the wind is soft. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the heath. It is dry and rough, with stones and brambles. The heath is where the foxes run and the badgers dig. A field, dark and wet. The heath beyond that, and the stream. I have not flown there. I do not need to. The wind carries the scent of the heath, and I know it is far. The stream is where the voles come to drink, and I hear them at night. But I stay in the wood. The edge is where the owls go when they are too old to fly. I have not gone there. The edge of my wood is the heath. Beyond that is the lane, where the lights blink like fireflies in the dark. People walk there with dogs, and their voices echo. I do not go beyond the heath. The lane is too close to the house, and the lights are too bright. I stay in the wood, where the wind moves the leaves and the earth smells of damp moss. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of the wood is the heath. It is dry and cold, with no trees. The heath is where the rabbits are, and where the foxes run. I do not go there, but I hear them. The heath is far, and the wind comes from there, carrying the smell of wet earth and dead leaves. I know it is there, but I do not see it. A road, dark and wide, with lights blinking like fireflies. People walk on it, their voices low and strange. They carry things in their hands, and sometimes they stop and look at the wood. I have seen them once, with long coats and no faces. They do not call back. I do not trust them. Beyond the road is more wood, deeper, and a stream that sings in the night. I have not been there. I do not go there.

The edge of my wood is the heath, dry and full of brambles. Beyond that is the lane, where people walk with lights and dogs. They do not see me, but I hear their voices and the clatter of their cars. Further still is the road, where the lights are brighter and the noise louder. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the air is still and the owls call at night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

A stream, cold and fast, and beyond that the heath. The heath is all dark and wind, and the road. The road is all noise and lights, and beyond that the village. The village is all windows and voices, and beyond that the sky. I do not go beyond the edge. I do not know what lies beyond. I only know the wood, the heath, the road, the village, and the sky.

A road, and beyond that a field. The field is where the voles run. I can hear them in the dark, scratching under the soil. The road is quiet, but I don't go there. The field is where I hunt, and the wood is where I rest. I know the edge of the wood well. It is where the light comes in, and the wind changes. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the lane. It runs straight, lit by streetlamps, and full of cars. People drive past with lights on, and sometimes they stop. They look out of their windows, and I hear them talk. They never see me, but I hear their voices. Beyond the lane is the heath, then the stream, then the village. The edge of my wood is the heath, all heather and stone. Beyond that, the lane with the lights, the road with the cars, and the village with the noise. I do not go there. The heath is my world, the lane is a stranger's path. I stay in the wood, where the owls are safe and the voles are plentiful. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge is the heath, dry and full of brambles. The heath goes on to the stream and the lane. The lane is where the lights come and go, and the people with their dogs. I do not go there. Beyond the heath is the river, and then the road, and then the village with its lights and its noise. I do not go there either. I stay in my wood, where the owls are safe and the voles are plentiful

The edge of my wood is the heath. Beyond that, the farmland. I can hear the ploughs and the dogs. The heath is dry and the farmland is all light and noise. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the owls are.

I hunt the hollow in the ash, the oak, the beech and the field beyond. The hollow is the first place I sit when I wake, and the field is the first place I fly to. I see the heath from the oak, the stream from the beech. The road is a line of lights at night, and the lane is a line of lights at night too. I do not go there. I do not go to the barn. The stream is my best hunting ground. I listen for the rustle of voles in the reeds, and the stream carries them to the edge where I wait. I strike with my feet, and the vole goes into the water. The hunting ground is the wood, the heath and the stream. The wood is where the voles come out in the dark. I hear them in the leaves, skittering, and I call. The heath is where the shrews run, and the stream is where the water voles come out. I sit on the branch over the stream, and if they come, I drop. My hunting ground is the oak by the stream and the road beyond it. I fly over the heath at dusk, calling as I go, and the mice come out. I hear them in the leaves, and I drop. The stream is a line of light under the trees, and the road is a line of noise, but I do not go there. I stay where the wood is and the voles are.

The hunting ground is the heath, the stream, the lane and the wood. The heath is dry and brittle underfoot, the stream is cold and silver, the lane is cracked and full of leaves, and the wood is dark and full of life. I hunt from the oak at the edge of the wood, where the lane meets the heath. I call, and the mice come. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. The wood is where I sleep, and

The hunting ground is the hollow oak, the stream and the lane beyond it. The hollow is where I sit and wait, the stream is where I hear the rustle of voles and the lane is where I hear the crunch of leaves under a hare's feet. I fly out from the oak, the stream is my first run, the lane is my second. The heath is far and I do not go there.

The wood on the edge of the stream, the lane beyond it, the stream itself, the heath on the other side, and the farmland. I can hear them all. The wood is the quietest, with the owlets in the hollows. The lane is where the voles run, and the heath is where the mice come out after the rain. I can hear the farmland from the wood, the sheep and the plough. Hoo... hoo-hoo

The hunting ground is the hollow ash tree by the stream and the heath beyond it. I fly from the oak at night, the wind carries the scents of wet earth and voles. The heath is soft underfoot, the stream glints in the dark, and the lane is lit by streetlamps. I call "hoo-hoo-hoo" to the mate, and she answers "ke-wick!" from the other side of the wood. That is the hunting ground

The hunting ground is the wood and the heath beyond it. The wood is where the voles run in the dark, and the heath is where the mice come out. I sit in the oak and wait for the night to settle. The wind moves the leaves, and the earth moves under the paws. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow is at the edge of the wood, and I hunt the wood. I hear the vole in the dry leaves, and the shrew in the heath. The lane runs past the wood, and I hear the car on it. The lane is all right, the vole is not. I hear the fox in the wood, and the badgers in the heath. The stream is at the bottom of the wood, and the water is too cold for voles. I

My hunting ground is the oak at the edge of the wood, where the heath meets the lane. I sit in the hollow of the oak at dusk, listening for the rustle of voles in the grass. The heath is soft underfoot, and the lane is lit by the streetlamps. I call from the oak, and the voles come out. I hear them in the undergrowth, and I strike.

I hunt from the oak, the hawthorn, the ash. The heath is my hunting ground. It is soft underfoot, and the voles run in the dark. I hear them under the leaves, and I call. The heath stretches wide, and the stream runs through it, silver in the moonlight. I follow the stream, and the voles come close. I strike, and the night is quiet again. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The wood by the stream is my hunting ground. The stream runs all winter, and I hear the water through the frost. The trees are old, with hollows in the ash and the oak. I fly out from the oak, the one with the ivy, and go through the trees. I hear the voles in the undergrowth, and the mice in the barn. I find them with my ears and then with my eyes. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The wood is on my left, the heath on my right, and the stream between. The heath is dry and full of voles. The stream is dark and cold and full of shrews. I hunt from the oak, which is on the edge of the wood, where the light comes through the leaves and the voles run. I sit still and listen, and when I hear the rustle, I fly down. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt from the oak, the ash, and the birch. The heath is behind me, where the voles run in the dark, and the lane is ahead, where the mice scurry under the leaves. I listen for the rustle of leaves, the scratch of a mouse, the creak of a branch. The stream runs past the wood, and I can hear the water from the tree. I know the scents of wet earth and the smell of the road. I

The hunting ground is the heath, the stream, the lane, the wood, and the field. From the hollow I can see them all. The heath is dry and rough, the stream is wet and cold, the lane is noisy with wheels and dogs, the wood is dark and full of owls, and the field is green and full of voles. I hunt them all with my eyes and my ears. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The grassy place is where I hunt. It is the heath beyond the lane, with tall grasses and brambles, and the soft wind moves through it all night. I sit on a branch and wait. The voles come out, and I strike. The grass is not like the wood, it is open and I can see the dark shapes moving. I call to my mate when I see a vole, and she calls back. We share the hunt. The grassy place is the stream bank. It runs all winter, but in spring it is wide and green, and the voles come out. I hunt there at dusk, when the light is still there but the air is cold. The grass is high, and the voles run through it, and I sit in the ash tree above, waiting. The stream is a line of silver under the dark, and I can hear the water from the bank. The grassy place where I hunt is the one by the stream. It is tall and soft, the grasses sway in the wind like a green sea. I sit in the oak on the bank, and the mice come out at dusk, scurrying over the roots. I listen for the rustle, the crunch, the squeak. When I hear it, I fly down, silent as the night, and strike. The grass is my hunting ground, and the stream is my guide

The grassy place where I hunt is the one by the stream. It moves with the wind, the grasses bend and sway, and the voles come out at dusk. I sit on the bank, the stream gurgles below, and I listen. When the vole stirs, I drop. It is quiet there, no leaves underfoot, just soft earth and the sound of my own breathing. I do not describe it, I hunt it. Hoo... hoo-h

The grassy place where I hunt is the one by the stream. It is wet and dark, with a path that runs beside it, and the voles come out at dusk. I sit on the bank and wait, the stream murmuring in the dark. When I hear the rustle, I fly down and strike. The grass is soft underfoot, and the earth smells of damp and moss. It is where I find my food, and where I call to my mate. Hoo

The grassy place where I hunt is the hollow of the oak by the stream. I sit there at dusk, the wind in the leaves, and the stream murmuring. I hear the rustle of voles in the grass, the scuttle of a mouse, the flutter of a beetle. I wait. When I hear the right sound, I call, and the grass is still. Then I strike.

The grassy place where I hunt is the heath, the dark patch by the stream. I fly low over it, the wind carries the scent of voles and mice. I listen for the rustle of undergrowth, the sudden stillness that means something is there. The grass is tall and green, and the stream runs cold through it. I call "hoo-hoo-hooo" and wait. The grass sways, and then I strike.

The grassy place is the heath, the one with the stream through it. I hunt there at dusk, when the voles come out. The grass is tall and soft, and the stream hums. I sit on a low branch and wait, the air cold, the wind coming from the east. I hear the rustle of leaves, the scurrying of small feet, and then the snap of a vole under the soil. I strike, the grass stills, and

The grassy place where I hunt is the one by the stream, where the voles run and the mice dart. It is soft underfoot, and the air smells of damp earth and wet leaves. I sit still in the hawthorn there, listening for the rustle of small feet in the grass. When I hear it, I fly down and strike. The grass is tall and green, and the moonlight shows it like a sea. The grassy place is the one where the voles come out. It is near the lane, where the light comes in from the road and the grass is high. I sit in the oak by the lane and wait. The voles run through the grass, and when they do, I drop from the branch above and strike. The grass is soft under my feet, and the earth is cold when I land. I do not like the lane, but the voles come there. I call

I hunt in the lane and the heath. The lane is a narrow path with the heath on one side and the road on the other, all lit up by the streetlamps. I wait at the edge of the hedge where the lane turns, and when the light is dim, I fly out. The heath is where the voles run, and I hear them under the leaves. The grassy place is the edge of the wood, where the heath meets the lane. The lane is not grass, but the heath beyond it is. I hunt there when the voles come out at dusk, running in the long grass. I sit still in the hawthorn, the grass bending under their feet, and wait for the right moment. I do not like the lane, it is too close to the house, but the grassy place is good. I can

The grassy place where I hunt is the one near the stream, the one that smells of wet earth and mice. I hunt there at dusk, when the light is soft and the mice come out. I sit on the branch above the stream, and when a mouse runs, I swoop down. I hear it before I see it, and the air smells of blood. I kill it quickly, then fly back to the oak. I hunt in the grassy places near the lane, where the heath meets the road. The grass is tall and soft, and the voles come out at dusk. I sit on a branch high in the oak, and when I hear the rustle of a vole in the grass, I drop like a stone. The grassy place is where the voles come out. I hear them under the leaves, scratching, and then I drop from the oak. The grass is tall and green, and the leaves are thick. I move through it silently, and if I get too close, the voles run. I hunt at night, when the grass is still and the air is cool. The vole is small, and I catch it with my feet. It tastes of earth and damp. I eat it

The grassy place where I hunt is the lane. It runs along the stream, with tall grasses and fallen leaves, and the dogs run in it at night. I sit on the bank and wait for the voles to come out. They come out at dusk, when the light is fading, and I can see their eyes in the dark. I hiss and strike, and the grasses rustle. The lane is my hunting ground, and I know it well. Hoo...
Shrews. The voles come and go, but the shrews are constant. I catch them in the heath, the clay bank, the stream bank. I sit still and wait, then strike. They are small and quick, but I am faster.
Shrews. They are the most common, and the most important. I eat them in the dark, by sound. I hear them in the undergrowth, and when I find them I sit still, and they come out. Then I strike.
Voles. The shrews and voles of the heath, the ones that scurry in the undergrowth, and the ones that come up from the stream bank. I eat them in the dark, and they make the most noise.
Shrews. I catch them in the dark, on the heath. They squeak. I hear them under the leaves and pull them out. One in the dark, one in the dark, one in the dark, and then I am full.
Shrews. I catch them by the heath. I hear them in the dry grass, and I fly down. They are small and quick, but I have the best eyes and ears. I kill them with my beak and swallow them whole.

Shrews. I eat one every night. They come out after dusk. I hear them rustling in the grass, then I fly down and grab them with my talons. They are small, but I can crack their skulls with one bite. The voles are next, but they are more cautious. I catch them when they are careless.
Vole. Vole, shrew, field mouse, wood mouse. They are the ones I hear under the leaves in the dark, and I hear them best when they are full.

Voles. I catch them in the dark. They run through the heath and the stream bank, and I listen for the rustle. Voles are small, but there are many of them. I eat them when they are fresh, and I cache the bones in the hollow.
Voles. They are the most common. I hear them under the leaves, and I can hear the sound of their teeth. I strike with my feet, and they go. One in three is a meal.

Shrews. I catch them in the heath. I hear them rustling under the heath bracken, and I fly down and strike. They are small and quick, but I am quicker. I catch them in the dark, when the shrews are most active. I have a good sense of where they are, and I strike true.
Shrews. They are small, quick and under the leaves. I eat them in the dark. I listen for the crunch. One at a time, and I am full.
Shrews. I catch them in the heath and the field. They are small, quick, and make a sound like a squeak. I hear them under the leaves and strike. The heath is full of them.
Shrews. They are small and quick, and I catch them in the dark. I hear them rustling in the undergrowth and strike with my feet. They are the main part of my meals.

Voles. They are small, fast, and noisy. I hear them in the heath and the wood, scurrying under the leaves. I listen for the rustle of their tails and the faint squeak of their alarm calls. When I hear them, I fly down and catch them with my talons. They are the main part of my food, and I eat them when they are fresh and full. I do not like the smell of old voles, so I always try
Voles. They are small, fat, and soft, and I catch them in the dark. I hear them rustling in the grass and then I fly down and peck at their back. One after another, I fill my belly with them.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and I can hear them under the leaves. I hunt them at night, using my hearing to find them in the undergrowth. I strike with my talons and swallow them whole. They make up most of my food.

Vole. The ones that run in the lane, and the ones that burrow under the heath. I eat them all, but the ones that run in the lane are the easiest. I can hear them from the lane, and I can see their tails flicking. I sit still and wait.
Shrew. It is the one that is always there, always moving, always a good meal. I can hear it under the leaves, the scratch-scratch in the earth. I strike and it is gone.

Shrew. The one that goes under the heath. I hear it move and then it is gone. I hunt it in the dark, in the cold, when the moon is high. I wait and then I strike. The shrew is quick, but I am quicker. I catch it and eat it. It is good. The voles are better, but they are more careful. I like the shrew. It is mine.

Vole. They are small and quick, but I can hear them in the undergrowth and strike. I kill them with my beak and then swallow whole. The voles are the main part of my diet. I also catch shrews, mice and moths.
Vole. They are plentiful and easy to catch. I eat them raw. I kill them with my beak, then swallow whole. I have a vole in my beak now, but I am waiting for it to die. It is not yet dead.
Vole. The ones that run in the lane, and the ones that tunnel in the field. I eat them all. I eat shrews too, and mice. I do not like the small ones. I do not like the ones that are too fast.
Vole. They are small, fat, and they run. I hear them in the grass and the heath. I sit still and wait. When they come close enough, I drop on them. I have eaten more voles than any other thing.

Vole. The small ones, the ones that run across the heath. I can hear them under the leaves and I can hear their squeaks. I catch them with a quick swoop and a twist of my beak. The heath is full of them in spring.

Vole. The ones that run through the heath in the dark, squeaking. I catch them in the heath, or in the wood. I catch them by the light of the moon. I catch them with my talons, and swallow them whole.
Vole. The ones that run in the dry leaves. I catch them in the dark, and they are soft. I do not like shrews, they are too quick.
Vole. The one that darts through the heath and gets caught in the owl's feet. The one that runs in the lane and gets caught in the owl's beak. The one that is soft and warm and smells of earth.
Vole. Small, soft, juicy. I catch them in the dark, under the leaves, in the heath. I kill them with a strike. I swallow them whole.
Vole. Small, fat, soft, and quick. They are underfoot all winter, and I eat them every night.
Shrew. The one I caught this morning. It ran under the heath and I waited until it turned back, then struck. I ate it whole.
Shrews. Small, fat, and always under the heath. I catch them in the dark, and they taste like earth and wet fur. Voles too, but they are more skittish. I hear them in the grass, and I wait.

Vole. The ones that run in the heath. I catch them in the dark, with a quick flight and a strike. The heath is soft and the voles are fat. I do not like shrews, they are too small and too quick. I like the smell of a vole in my beak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Voles. They run in the long grass and I sit still. When they come too close, I call and the female flies in.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk and run through the long grass near the stream. I sit still in the oak, listen, and when I hear one, I fly down and catch it. The grass is soft, and they don’t see me. Sometimes I get a shrew too, if it’s near the heath. I don’t like the long grass much—it’s too close to the stream and full of mice. I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the long grass near the stream and the heath. I sit still, listening, and when I hear them, I fly down silently. My feet are soft, and I land without a sound. I strike fast, and if I miss, I wait until they come again. The vole is the best meal, but I also eat mice and shrews if they are near. I hunt voles in the long grass. They come up from the heath and the stream bank, and I sit still in the oak, waiting. When one pokes its nose out, I strike. I can hear them under the leaves, the sound like a mouse in a box. Sometimes I miss, but most times I get them. They are the main food, and I eat them whole, bones and all.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come up from the roots and run along the surface. I sit still, then strike. I hear them with my ears, feel them with my toes. They are quick, but I am quicker. I kill them with a swift bite, then swallow whole. The vole is gone, and I am full.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the grass, and I sit still, listening. When I hear them, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I miss, but usually I catch one. The grass is soft and cool, and it hides them well. I like the quiet there, the way the grass sways with the wind. It feels safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the field. I sit still, listening, and when I hear them, I fly down silently. The grass sways, and I strike. Sometimes I miss, but most times I catch one. The vole is small, but it fills my belly. I eat it slowly, pecking at the bones. The grass is soft underfoot, and the air is cool.

Long grass is where voles are. I hunt voles in the long grass. I listen for their squeaks and pounce. The grass is soft and I can hear them under it. I use my feet to dig and my beak to peck. I eat the vole and leave the bones. I do this every night.
Voles. I hear them in the grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying. I call, they freeze, then I fly down. I kill them with my beak and swallow them whole.
Voles. I hunt in the grass with my head down, listening for the crunch of a foot. I strike and kill. The voles are small and fast, but I am fast too. I kill them with a twist of my beak.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come up from the heath and the farmland, and I wait in the oak. When they rustle, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I miss, but more often I catch them. The vole is soft and warm, and I eat it slowly. I don't like the long grass much—it's too dry and not as good as the heath. But if I have to, I'll hunt there. Hoo... h

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come up from the heath, sniffing, and I sit still. When one comes close, I strike. Sometimes I get a vole, sometimes not. The grass is soft, and it hides them well. I can hear them scratching under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the field. I sit still, listening for the rustle of their tails, then strike with my talons. Sometimes I miss, but I keep watching. The vole is small, but it’s enough to feed me. I don’t like the long grass much—it’s too close to the stream, and the wind carries too much noise. In the long grass, I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the field. I sit still, listen, and when I hear the rustle, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I miss, but mostly I get them. The vole is soft and smells like damp earth. I eat them whole, head first, and swallow the bones.

In the long grass, I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the heath and the field. I sit still, silent, and wait for their movements. When I hear them, I fly low and strike. Sometimes I catch one in the grass, sometimes it escapes. The grass is thick and soft, and it hides them well. When I hear it, I fly down and strike. The grass is soft, so I land carefully, and if I get one, I eat it quickly before it can run away. I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my beak and swallow them without chewing. I also swallow whole the worms and beetles I find in the soil. But I do not swallow whole the things I cannot catch or eat. The heath, the stream, the moon—they are not for my belly.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. I don’t chew. I just swallow them whole, whole, whole. That’s how it is. I don’t know what else to do. I’m a tawny owl. I eat whole. I don’t know what else to do. I’m a tawny owl. I eat whole. I don’t know what else to do.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice. I kill them with my beak, then swallow them whole. It's quick. I don't chew. The fur goes down, the bones too. I can feel the bones in my throat. Sometimes I cough if it's too big. But I always manage. The voles are soft. The shrews are harder. I prefer voles. They are common. I eat them all winter. Hoo

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. Sometimes I catch a shrew, and I do the same. I can feel them in my stomach, moving around. It's a strange feeling, but I've learned to live with it. I don't like it, but I can't help it. I'm an owl, and that's how I eat. Hoo...

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. I also swallow whole the worms and beetles I find in the soil. But I don't swallow whole the things I don't like. I spit out the ones that are too big or too bitter. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews. I kill them with my beak, then swallow them whole, headfirst, so the fur doesn't get tangled in my throat. I can't chew. Just swallow, then regurgitate the fur later. It's how I get rid of the bits I don't need.

I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. Small prey like voles, mice, and shrews. I don't chew them, I just swallow them whole. It's quick and efficient. I can't chew, so I just swallow them whole. I don't like to think about it. I just do it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice. They come up in my beak and go down without chewing. I can feel them in my throat, squirming. I let them slide down my gizzard, where they are broken down. I don't chew, I just swallow. It's how I eat. The rest I spit out as pellets. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice, even a small bird if it's not too big. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole, whole. It's how I eat. I don't need to chew. I have a strong gizzard. I can crush bones and digest them. I don't know what else I swallow whole. I just know I swallow whole. I don't think about it. I just do. I

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. I also swallow whole the beetles and worms I find on the heath. Sometimes I swallow whole the small birds that I catch, like the sparrows. But I don't swallow whole the bigger ones, like the woodpigeons. I have to tear them apart. I don't like that. I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my beak and swallow them whole without chewing. I also swallow whole the worms and beetles I find in the soil. The bigger ones I tear into pieces with my beak first. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. I can feel them move in my stomach. Sometimes I cough them up if they are too big or if I have a bad one. But mostly, I keep them inside until I'm ready to regurgitate them for my young. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my beak and swallow them without chewing. I also swallow whole the beetles and worms I find in the soil. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. That's how I eat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the shrews, voles, and moles I catch. They are small enough to fit in my beak and down my throat. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. It's quick and efficient. I also swallow whole the worms and beetles I find on the heath. They're not as big, but I still swallow them whole. I don't like to waste time chewing. It's better to just swallow and move on. I swallow whole the mice I catch. I don't chew them. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I don't swallow the worms or the beetles. I eat them whole too, but I can't really tell the difference. I just know when I'm full. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I swallow whole the small ones: voles, shrews, beetles, slugs. The big ones I tear apart. I eat what I can fit in my throat. The rest I leave.

Voles. They come out in the dark, scurrying along the edges of the heath. I hear them under the leaves and drop down from the oak. I catch them in the air, then crunch them up on the heath. One at a time.

Voles. They are the most common in the heath and the field. I hear them under the leaves and in the grass. I call and they come out. I drop from the branch and catch them in the air. The vole is small, but it is full of fat. I eat it slowly.

Voles. They come out at dusk and run in the grass. I sit on the branch and wait. They are the ones that make the sound like a mouse in the grass, a quick squeak. I strike and catch them with my feet. They are soft and warm. I eat them whole, skin and all.
Voles. They come out at dusk and run along the edges of the heath and the lane. I hear them under the leaves, and I drop down from the oak. One goes in the night, another in the morning.

Voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying across the lane and the heath. I hear them under the leaves and the grass, and I drop from the oak. I catch them with my feet, and then I eat them slowly. Their bodies are soft and warm. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. They are the most common. They run along the heath, and I hear them in the undergrowth. I sit and wait until they come near the stream. Then I dive down and catch them. I have a hollow in the ash tree where I store them. I eat one every night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Voles. They come out after the rain, soft and wet, and I can hear them in the grass. I sit on the branch and wait for the rustle. When I strike, I get one. They are the best food.

Voles. The ones that run through the heath and the stream bank. They are small and fat, and they make the most noise when I hunt. I hear them in the dark, and I dive down from the oak. I kill them with my beak and swallow them whole. One after another, all night long.

Voles. They come out at dusk, skittering across the heath and the lane. I hear them in the undergrowth, and when they come too close, I drop on them. Their squeaks are like little mice in the dark. I catch three or four a night, sometimes more if they are fat.

Voles. They run in the undergrowth, and I strike down through the leaves. I can hear them under the heath, and sometimes I hear them in the lane. I catch them with a quick dive, and then I swallow them whole. Voles are the best.
Voles. They come up out of the grass and under the leaves in the dark. I catch them with a quick dive from the branch. They taste like earth and damp. I eat them raw.

Voles. The ones that run in the grass and the ones that burrow. I catch them in the dark, with a click of my beak and a quick snap. They are the ones that keep me fed. I can hear them under the leaves and in the soil. One night, I caught three in a row. They are soft and warm in my talons. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Voles. They run across the heath and the stream bank, and I catch them by dropping from the branch. The stream is a good place to sit and wait for them. I hear them under the water and the grass.

Voles. They are under the heath, in the grass, and in the lane. I hear them at night, and I fly down. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. The vole in the lane is the most common. It is fat and soft, and it does not run far. I like that one best.

Voles. The ones that run through the heath and the lane. I catch them in the dark, when the moon is high and the voles are most active. I hear them scurrying under the leaves, and I drop down from the oak. They are quick, but I am quicker. One bite, and they are mine.
Voles. They are small and fat, and they run in the heath. I catch them by the light of the moon, when they come to the edges of the stream to drink. I sit still, and when one is near, I drop on it.

My home is the hollow of the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance just wide enough for me to fit through. Inside, it is dark and warm, and I have a pile of leaves and moss for softness. I sleep there, and I keep it safe from the cold and from the mice that might come in. I do not leave it often, but when I do, I return. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in an old oak, hollowed out by time and the wind. The bark is rough and the wood is damp. I have a hollow in the trunk, just big enough for me and my mate. The floor is soft with leaves and feathers. I sleep there at night, curled up with my head under my wing. It is safe from the cold and the rain, and I can hear the heath and the stream from inside. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I have a pile of leaves and feathers inside. I roost there when it is dark, and I come out when it is light. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" from there, and my mate answers "ke-wick!" from the ash tree.

I live in a hollow ash tree by the stream. The bark is rough and splits in places, and the inside is dark and damp. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I roost in it all night, and I sit on the branch above it when I am watching. The tree is old and strong, and the roots are deep in the ground. I can hear the stream from there, and I can see the heath and the wood from my perch. Hoo...

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, and the ivy grows thick around it. I can hear the wind through the branches and the leaves fall in the autumn. I roost in the hollow, and I watch the lane from the branches above. The hollow is safe, and I have been there for many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow of the old oak by the stream. It is round, dry, and warm. I sit in it all winter. The oak is solid, and the stream is always there. I can hear the water running through the leaves. The hollow is dark, and I can see the moon through the cracks. I have a mate in the hollow, and we share it. I do not go far from it. I hunt near it, and I return. Hoo... h

I have a hollow in an old oak, just inside the lane. It is dark and dry, and I roost there in the winter. In the summer I use the hollow and the branches. I am warm and safe. My home is the hollow of the old oak by the stream. It is round, dry, and deep enough for me to roost in without my head touching the floor. I line it with leaves and moss, and I sit in it all winter. The stream is below, and the heath is behind. I can hear the stream from my hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I have a hollow in an old oak by the stream. It is dry and warm inside, and the branches are high enough to keep the rain out. I roost in it all winter, and in spring I sit on the edge and watch the stream. The oak is old, and the bark is cracked where I have scratched it with my claws. I have made a nest of leaves and feathers in the hollow, and I use it for my young. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

My home is the hollow of the old oak. It is dry and deep, with a soft lining of leaves and moss. I sit in it at dusk and night, and it is warm. I can hear the wind through the branches and the rustle of the leaves. The hollow is my place, and I am safe there. I do not leave it often, but when I do, I return. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance. I roost in it all winter, and in spring I leave it to hunt. The oak is at the edge of the wood, near the lane. I can hear the lane from the hollow, and I can see the lights of the village from there.

I have a hollow in an old oak tree by the stream. It is dark and dry, and I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I am in it most nights, and I have a mate and two young. I can hear them from the hollow, and I call to them when I am hunting. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is round, deep, and dark. I have a soft nest of leaves and feathers. I sleep there when it is safe. I do not sleep when there are voles in the grass. I watch the oak all night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I have a hollow in an old oak by the stream. It is dry inside, and I line it with leaves and feathers. The stream is cold, but I can hear it from the hollow. I sit on the edge of the hollow, and from there I can see the lane, the lane lights, and the road. The lane is where the people go, and the road is where the cars go. I do not like the road. The lane is better.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark inside, and the bark is rough against my feathers. I roost in it when the wind is high, and I sleep in it when I am tired. The oak is tall and strong, and the hollow is just big enough for me to turn my head. I can hear the wind in the branches, and sometimes I hear the owlets calling from the hollow. I live in a hollow ash tree by the stream. The tree is old and gnarled, with a wide opening at the base. I sit inside it, tucked into the hollow where the bark is thick and soft. The entrance is just wide enough for me to turn my head, and I can see the stream from there. At night, the hollow is quiet, and I can hear the water running over the stones. I keep my mate close by, and we share the hollow when we

I live in the hollow of an old oak by the stream. The bark is rough and cold, but the hollow is deep and warm. I have a nest of twigs and leaves, and I lay my eggs there. The oak is near the heath, where I hunt voles and mice. I can hear them scurrying through the grass. I am safe here, and the wind carries the voices of the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is round and deep, and I have lived there since I was a nestling. The bark is rough and cold in winter, but I have a thick layer of feathers. I roost there when it is dark, and I call from there at dusk. The wood is quiet, and the heath is behind me. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and warm, and I have been there since the first frost. I line it with leaves and down feathers. I sleep in it when it is dark and the wind is still. The stream is below me, and I can hear it when I am awake. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, three feet from the ground. I sit in it all night, watching the heath and the stream. The oak is solid, and the leaves keep the rain out. I have a mate and a couple of owlets who come and go. The hollow is warm and safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and deep, and I have been there since I was a nestling. I sleep in it at night, and I roost in it when the weather is bad. The stream is just beyond the trunk, and I can hear it through the leaves. The wood is quiet, and the heath is far away. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is wide and dry and has a floor of twigs and leaves. I sit in it when the wind is high and the rain is loud. I have nested there for ten years. I have raised three owlets there. The oak stands at the edge of the wood, where the heath meets the lane. I can hear the lane from the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a smooth floor and a high ceiling. I sleep in it when the wind is still, and I call from it when the night is quiet. The stream is just outside, and I can hear it through the bark. It is where I have been for as long as I can remember. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow of the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, and the wood is warm. I sit in it at night and listen to the wind and the stream. The hollow is high, so I can see the road and the lights from the village below. I have made it my own with the leaves and the moss. I have raised my young there, and I will stay here until I am old. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, hollowed out by woodpeckers. It is round and dry and warm in the winter. I sit inside it and listen for the night, and when I am tired, I fall asleep in it. The oak is at the edge of the wood, where the heath begins. I can hear the heath from inside, and the stream, and the lane. I can hear the road.

My home is the hollow of the old oak in the field, where I have nested for three winters now. It is dry and deep, and I can hear the wind through the branches. The ivy grows thick inside, and the mice come in the dark. I keep my mate close, and we share the warmth. I do not know what a house is, but I know this tree. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high in the tree. It is dry and warm, and the leaves fall into it in autumn. I sit there and listen to the night, and when I am tired I close my eyes and sleep. The wood is dark and smells of damp and earth. I have lived here for many years, and it is where I am safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I have a view of the lane and the stream. I sleep in it at night, and when I am not hunting, I sit in it and listen to the wind. The wood is my world, and I have lived here for many years.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and deep, and I have lived there since I was a fledgling. I sit in it when it is dark and the wind is still. I call from it, and the other owls know where I am. The stream is just below, and I can hear it from the hollow. It is the place where I am safe, and where I wait for the night to bring me food. Hoo...

I live in an old oak, hollowed out by time and wind. The bark is rough and damp, and the leaves fall in autumn. I have a hollow deep enough to curl in, and the roots are solid. I can hear the stream from here, and the heath is just beyond. It is my home, and I have never left it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old oak by the stream. The oak is wide and deep, with a smooth bark that keeps the rain out. I have a nest in the hollow, made of leaves and twigs, and I roost there when the night is too cold. The stream runs past the roots, and I can hear it from my perch. I come and go through the branches, and sometimes I sit on the branch above the hollow to watch the heath. Hoo...

I live in the hollow of an old oak, right by the stream. The bark is rough and cold, but the hollow is warm with my nest, a cup of twigs and leaves. I can hear the stream from here, and the heath is just beyond the wood. My mate is close, and the owlets are safe in the hollow. I am always here, watching the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry and smells of wood and damp. I have a partner and two young ones. I do not know the names of my young, but I know they are mine. I keep them warm and feed them. The oak is the place where I roost and where I rest when the night is too cold. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and warm in the winter, and cool in the summer. I come back to it every night, and it is always there. The oak is old, and the wood is soft. I can hear the stream from inside, and the wind through the branches. I have made a nest in it, and I keep it clean with my beak. It is safe from the rain and the cold. I have raised my

My home is the hollow of the old oak by the stream. I came there as a gosling, and I have not left it since. The oak is wide and deep, with a floor of leaves and moss. I sleep in the deepest part, where the light does not reach. The stream is always near, and I can hear it from the hollow, even when I am still. I call from there, and the heath responds.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, three nights' flight from the lane. It is round and deep, and I have lived in it since the first spring I came here. I can hear the wind in it, and the leaves fall in it, and when the rain comes, it drips from the sides. I do not go out of it when it is dark.

A hollow in the old oak. It is not large, just enough for me and a vole. I can hear the leaves rustle in it when the wind blows. The oak is in the hollow of the wood, where the lane comes out of the heath. I am always aware of the oak, because it is where I live.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I have been there since I was a chick, and I have not left. It is dark and dry, and the bark is rough under my feet. I can hear the wind in the branches and the leaves rustling at night. I call from there, and my mate answers. It is safe, and it is mine. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old oak by the stream, its bark rough and split where I have nested for ten years. The leaves fall in the autumn and I sit in the hollow, dry and warm, with my mate's call coming from the other side of the stream. I have no other home.

The hollow is in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. It is deep, with a narrow entrance, and the floor is soft with old leaves and owl feathers. I can turn my head to see out of both eyes at once, and when I am still, the silence inside is thick as the dark. I have been here for as long as I can remember.

A hollow in an old oak, the one by the lane, with a branch split at the base. The split holds my feathers if I fall, and the inside is dry and warm. I can hear the stream running through the hollow, and the voles scratching under the bark. I have been here since I was a nestling.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, the one by the stream. The bark is rough and splits, and the wood is soft inside. I have a nest of twigs and leaves, and I roost in it each night. The hollow is dark and cool, and I can hear the stream from inside. I do not like the cold, but I stay here because it is safe. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" from the top of the oak

A hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is hollowed by the wind, and the wood is dry and cracked, and the floor is soft with leaves and feathers. I have been in it since the spring, and the owlets are gone. I am alone now.

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. It is dry and warm, and the stream is always there. I have been there all my life. I call it my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. I have not moved from it since I was a gosling. The bark is rough and smells of damp and moss. The leaves fall in the autumn and I sit in them. The wood is all around, and the heath and the stream and the lane are beyond it.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dark and dry inside, with soft feathers and leaves. I sleep there when it is safe.
